name: Şeyh Galip
bio: Mehmed Esad, known as Şeyh Galip or Galib Dede (1757–1799), was a Mevlevi dervish and sheikh of the Galata convent in Istanbul, and one of the foremost poets of the late Ottoman Romantic school. Sultan Selim III conferred on him the office of sheikh.

His masterpiece is the mystical romance Husn ü Aşk ('Beauty and Love'), from which two passages are given here. E. J. W. Gibb, who gave the first English account of his diwan, praised the strong and glowing verse of his lyric poems.

poems.title: While the Lovers Circle Here in Mystic Dance
poems.author: Şeyh Galip
poems.collection: A History of Ottoman Poetry, vol. IV (1905)
poems.note: A ghazel on the sema, the mystic whirling dance of the Mevlevi dervishes, in which the heavens and the lovers turn together. Gibb's notes explain the sema and the 'Heavenly Birds' who are moved by the Mevlevi reed-flute.
poems.text:
While the lovers circle here in mystic dance,
Sun and moon traverse the sphere in mystic dance.

Love's deep secret made the spheric heavens reel;
All the worlds do still appear in mystic dance.

E'en as 'twere a whirlpool shows the weeping eye,
Casting pearls and spray as clear in mystic dance.

Youthful Magians sweet about the Tavern go,
Like as pilgrims round in fere in mystic dance.

Lo, the reed ecstatic thrills, the Heavenly Birds
Dove-like beat their plumy gear in mystic dance.

I am yonder vagrant Qays upon whose head
Whiles the nests do leap and rear in mystic dance.

Ghalib, while the Sun of Love doth radiance pour,
Mevlevis will mote-like veer in mystic dance.

poems.title: Those Cries That Sound Throughout the Fast
poems.author: Şeyh Galip
poems.collection: A History of Ottoman Poetry, vol. IV (1905)
poems.note: A devotional ghazel addressed to God, in which every cry, song and cup of the convent is said to belong to Him alone. Gibb's notes explain the dervishes' ecstatic cry 'Yâ Hû', meaning 'Oh He', which refers to God.
poems.text:
Those cries that sound throughout the fast as for the bowl are all for Thee;
Those songs and roundelays the which the minstrels troll are all for Thee.

O world-illuming Sun, look down for once upon the rose of hope;
Those radiant beauties sheen as dewy aureole are all for Thee.

O King, what though Thou deign'st to honour with Thy face the dervish poor?
Those shouts of Hay! and Hû! that through this convent roll are all for Thee.

Intent to catch the lustrous pearls of Thy dear words those eager ears
That shell-like open wide and list from heart and soul are all for Thee.

All single-handed how to clutch the skirt of my poor heart's desire?
Those cruel dagger-lashes fain to work my dole are all for Thee.

The vines are scattered all around with purpose fair of quaffing wine;
Those shatterings of the cup, those cares to keep it whole, are all for Thee.

The while in Ghalib's walk there be no trace of aught suspicious seen,
Those reverences fore the Elder of the Bowl are all for Thee.

poems.title: Out on This Jugglery
poems.author: Şeyh Galip
poems.collection: A History of Ottoman Poetry, vol. IV (1905)
poems.note: A ghazel on the vanity of pomp and power, in which every worldly show is cursed in turn, from the pasha's horse-hair standard to the candle on the tomb. Gibb's notes explain the tugh, the horse-hair standard that marked a pasha's rank.
poems.text:
Out on this jugglery! by God! out on this idle snare!
Out on this pomp and circumstance! out on this glory and glare!

Since never pasha finds a rag to shroud his lopped off head,
Out on his flag of honour, his badge of horse's hair!

Since ever must the blast of death blow out the lamp of life.
Out on the useless candle that above the tomb doth flare!

How often often have I traced it on the page of earth!
Out on this form of nights and days for aye repeated there!

A mansion whose foundation rests on sighs and bitter tears;
Woe for such show and bravery! out on such beauty fair!

From torment's furnace let them issue forth mid sweat of pain,
Out on them all, these regal pearls, these rubies pure and rare!

To those who, erst of high estate, their rank have forfeited
'Out on thee!' groans the rumbling drum, and 'Out!' the tabor's blare.

Since that the wedding-revelry must turn to mourning's gloom,
Pugh for the taper of the feast! out on the flambeau-glare!

O Ghalib, be thou dervish-souled, seek poverty's retreat;
Take flute in hand and play, then out on Fortune everywhere!

The while that at Our Master's gate I find my hopes I'll sing:
'Out on the stress and anguish which from earth's duresse I bear!'

poems.title: We Reached the Loved One's Blissful Gate
poems.author: Şeyh Galip
poems.collection: A History of Ottoman Poetry, vol. IV (1905)
poems.note: A mystic ghazel of the seeker who reaches the gate of the Beloved and even Paradise, yet finds no vision, and ends at the divan of Love itself. Gibb's notes explain the Beatific Vision and the fourth sphere as the 'station' of Jesus.

poems.title: The Song of Love's Nurse
poems.author: Şeyh Galip
poems.note: A lullaby sung by Love's nurse in Galib's Husn ü Aşk, in which the child beauties, the Moon, the Rosebud and the Narcissus, are warned of the cruelty of Fate that is to come.

poems.title: Sweet Were Those Moments When the Heart Was Gay
poems.author: Şeyh Galip
poems.note: A lament from Husn ü Aşk for the lover's happy days, now ruined by parting, when the wine and the company of the beloved are gone.
